For the galvanic cell involving the reaction
$\mathrm{Ni(s)} + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Ni}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Cu(s)}$
the standard cell potential ($E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$) is $0.59 \text{ V}$ at $298 \text{ K}$. Calculate the logarithm of the equilibrium constant ($\log K_c$) for the cell reaction.
(Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.059 \text{ V}$ at $298 \text{ K}$)
questions.question:
For the galvanic cell involving the reaction
$\mathrm{Ni(s)} + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Ni}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Cu(s)}$
the standard cell potential ($E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$) is $0.59 \text{ V}$ at $298 \text{ K}$. Calculate the logarithm of the equilibrium constant ($\log K_c$) for the cell reaction.
(Given: $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.059 \text{ V}$ at $298 \text{ K}$)
questions.solution:
The relationship between standard cell potential and equilibrium constant is given by the Nernst equation at equilibrium:
$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \dfrac{2.303 RT}{nF} \log K_c$

For the given reaction, $\mathrm{Ni}$ is oxidized to $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ is reduced to $\mathrm{Cu}$. The number of electrons transferred, $n = 2$.

Substituting the given values into the equation:
$0.59 = \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log K_c$

$\log K_c = \dfrac{0.59 \times 2}{0.059}$

$\log K_c = 10 \times 2 = 20$

Using $n=1$ leads to the incorrect value of $10$, and confusing the sign with the $\Delta G^\circ$ formula leads to $-20$.

Answer: $20$

questions.question: The limiting molar conductivities of $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$, $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and $\text{NaOH}$ are $271.6$, $149.7$ and $248.1 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ respectively. What is the limiting molar conductivity of $\text{NaCl}$?
questions.solution:
According to Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions:
$\Lambda^\circ_m(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}) = \Lambda^\circ_m(\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}) + \Lambda^\circ_m(\text{NaOH}) - \Lambda^\circ_m(\text{NaCl})$

Rearranging the equation to solve for $\Lambda^\circ_m(\text{NaCl})$:
$\Lambda^\circ_m(\text{NaCl}) = \Lambda^\circ_m(\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}) + \Lambda^\circ_m(\text{NaOH}) - \Lambda^\circ_m(\text{NH}_4\text{OH})$

Substituting the given values:
$\Lambda^\circ_m(\text{NaCl}) = 149.7 + 248.1 - 271.6$
$\Lambda^\circ_m(\text{NaCl}) = 397.8 - 271.6 = 126.2 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $126.2 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$

questions.q:
The mass of aluminium deposited at the cathode when a current of 9.65 A is passed through molten aluminium chloride for 1000 seconds is:
(Given: Molar mass of $\mathrm{Al} = 27 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}, 1 \mathrm{~F} = 96500 \mathrm{~C}$)
questions.question:
The mass of aluminium deposited at the cathode when a current of 9.65 A is passed through molten aluminium chloride for 1000 seconds is:
(Given: Molar mass of $\mathrm{Al} = 27 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}, 1 \mathrm{~F} = 96500 \mathrm{~C}$)
questions.solution:
The reduction reaction at the cathode for molten aluminium chloride is:
$\mathrm{Al}^{3+} + 3\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{s})$

Here, the number of moles of electrons required per mole of Al is $n = 3$.

According to Faraday's First Law of Electrolysis:
$w = \dfrac{M \times I \times t}{n \times F}$

Given:
$M = 27 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
$I = 9.65 \mathrm{~A}$
$t = 1000 \mathrm{~s}$
$F = 96500 \mathrm{~C}$

Substituting the values:
$w = \dfrac{27 \times 9.65 \times 1000}{3 \times 96500}$

$w = \dfrac{27 \times 9650}{289500}$

$w = \dfrac{27}{30} = 0.9 \mathrm{~g}$

Thus, the mass of aluminium deposited is $0.9 \mathrm{~g}$.

Answer: 0.9 g

Answer: $25$

$\left(\text{Given}: \dfrac{2.303\ RT}{F} = 0.059\right)$
questions.question:
A galvanic cell consists of a Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) as the cathode and another hydrogen electrode ($P_{\text{H}_2} = 1$ atm) dipped in an unknown acidic solution as the anode. If the measured cell potential is $0.236$ V at $298$ K, what is the pH of the unknown solution?
$\left(\text{Given}: \dfrac{2.303\ RT}{F} = 0.059\right)$
questions.solution:
The cell can be represented as:
$\text{Pt (s)} | \text{H}_2 \text{(g, 1 atm)} | \text{H}^{+} \text{(aq, unknown)} \ || \ \text{H}^{+} \text{(aq, 1 M)} | \text{H}_2 \text{(g, 1 atm)} | \text{Pt (s)}$

The cell potential is given by:
$E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{cathode}} - E_{\text{anode}}$

For the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (cathode):
$E_{\text{cathode}} = 0$ V

For the anode (reduction potential):
$E_{\text{anode}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log \dfrac{P_{\text{H}_2}}{[\text{H}^{+}]^2}$
$E_{\text{anode}} = 0 - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log \dfrac{1}{[\text{H}^{+}]^2}$
$E_{\text{anode}} = - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \times (-2 \log [\text{H}^{+}])$
$E_{\text{anode}} = 0.059 \log [\text{H}^{+}] = -0.059 \text{ pH}$

Substituting into the cell potential equation:
$E_{\text{cell}} = 0 - (-0.059 \text{ pH}) = 0.059 \text{ pH}$

Given $E_{\text{cell}} = 0.236$ V:
$0.236 = 0.059 \text{ pH}$
$\text{pH} = \dfrac{0.236}{0.059} = 4$

Using $\dfrac{0.059}{2}$ directly for the pH relation leads to an incorrect pH of 8, and a sign error leads to -4.

Answer: $4$

questions.solution:
The cell reaction is:
$\text{Zn(s)} + 2\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + \text{H}_{2}(\text{g})$

The standard cell potential is:
$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 0.00 - (-0.76) = 0.76\text{ V}$

The number of electrons transferred, $n = 2$.

Using the Nernst equation:
$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0.059}{n} \log \dfrac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]P_{\text{H}_{2}}}{[\text{H}^{+}]^{2}}$

Substitute the given values:
$0.642 = 0.76 - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log \dfrac{0.1 \times 1}{[\text{H}^{+}]^{2}}$

$0.642 = 0.76 - 0.0295 \log \dfrac{10^{-1}}{[\text{H}^{+}]^{2}}$

$0.76 - 0.642 = 0.0295 (\log 10^{-1} - \log [\text{H}^{+}]^{2})$

$0.118 = 0.0295 (-1 - 2\log [\text{H}^{+}])$

Since $\text{pH} = -\log [\text{H}^{+}]$, we can write $-2\log [\text{H}^{+}] = 2\text{pH}$:
$0.118 = 0.0295 (-1 + 2\text{pH})$

$\dfrac{0.118}{0.0295} = -1 + 2\text{pH}$

$4 = -1 + 2\text{pH}$

$2\text{pH} = 5 \Rightarrow \text{pH} = 2.5$

Forgetting to square the $[\text{H}^{+}]$ term leads to an incorrect pH of $5.0$, while using $n=1$ leads to $1.5$.

Answer: $2.5$

(Given: Molar mass of $\mathrm{Cu} = 63.5 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$, $\mathrm{Ag} = 108 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
According to Faraday's Second Law of Electrolysis, when the same quantity of electricity is passed through different electrolytes connected in series, the masses of the substances deposited are proportional to their respective equivalent weights.

$\dfrac{w_{\mathrm{Ag}}}{w_{\mathrm{Cu}}} = \dfrac{E_{\mathrm{Ag}}}{E_{\mathrm{Cu}}}$

The equivalent weight of a metal is its molar mass divided by its valency (n-factor).
For $\mathrm{Ag}$ in $\mathrm{AgNO}_3$, valency $= 1$
$E_{\mathrm{Ag}} = \dfrac{108}{1} = 108$

For $\mathrm{Cu}$ in $\mathrm{CuSO}_4$, valency $= 2$
$E_{\mathrm{Cu}} = \dfrac{63.5}{2} = 31.75$

Substituting the values into the ratio:
$\dfrac{w_{\mathrm{Ag}}}{1.27} = \dfrac{108}{31.75}$

$w_{\mathrm{Ag}} = 1.27 \times \dfrac{108}{31.75} = 1.27 \times 3.4015...$

Alternatively, calculate the number of equivalents of Cu deposited:
Equivalents of $\mathrm{Cu} = \dfrac{1.27}{31.75} = 0.04$

Equivalents of $\mathrm{Ag}$ deposited $= 0.04$
Mass of $\mathrm{Ag} = 0.04 \times 108 = 4.32 \mathrm{~g}$

Answer: $4.32 \mathrm{~g}$

Consequently, the limiting molar conductivity ($\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}$) for weak electrolytes cannot be obtained by simply extrapolating the curve to zero concentration (as is done for strong electrolytes). Instead, Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions is used.

Therefore, the correct description is that its molar conductivity increases steeply at lower concentrations and its $\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}$ cannot be obtained by extrapolation.

(Given : Molar volume of a gas at STP $= 22.4$ L mol$^{-1}$; $1$ F $= 96500$ C mol$^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
The quantity of charge $Q$ passed through the solution is:
$Q = I \times t = 9.65 \text{ A} \times (10 \times 60) \text{ s} = 5790 \text{ C}$

The oxidation reaction at the anode is:
$2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{O}_2(g) + 4\text{H}^{+}(aq) + 4\text{e}^{-}$

This indicates that $4$ moles of electrons ($4$ F of charge) are required to produce $1$ mole of $\text{O}_2$ gas. Thus, the n-factor for oxygen gas evolution is $4$.

Number of moles of $\text{O}_2$ produced $= \dfrac{Q}{n \times F} = \dfrac{5790}{4 \times 96500} = \dfrac{5790}{386000} = 0.015 \text{ mol}$

Volume of $\text{O}_2$ gas at STP $= \text{moles} \times \text{Molar volume}$
$V = 0.015 \text{ mol} \times 22.4 \text{ L mol}^{-1} = 0.336 \text{ L}$

Converting to millilitres:
$V = 0.336 \times 1000 = 336 \text{ mL}$

Answer: $336$ mL

What is the standard cell potential ($E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$) for the disproportionation reaction of $\text{Au}^+$?

questions.solution:
The disproportionation reaction is $3\text{Au}^+ \rightarrow \text{Au}^{3+} + 2\text{Au}$.
This involves two half-reactions:
Oxidation: $\text{Au}^+ \rightarrow \text{Au}^{3+} + 2e^-$
Reduction: $\text{Au}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Au}$

First, calculate the standard reduction potential for $\text{Au}^{3+}/\text{Au}^+$:
$\text{Au}^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow \text{Au}$, $E^\circ_1 = +1.40$ V, $\Delta G^\circ_1 = -3F(1.40) = -4.20F$
$\text{Au}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Au}$, $E^\circ_2 = +1.69$ V, $\Delta G^\circ_2 = -1F(1.69) = -1.69F$

The target half-reaction is $\text{Au}^{3+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Au}^+$.
This is obtained by subtracting the second reaction from the first:
$\Delta G^\circ_3 = \Delta G^\circ_1 - \Delta G^\circ_2 = -4.20F - (-1.69F) = -2.51F$
$-2FE^\circ_3 = -2.51F \implies E^\circ_3 = +1.255$ V.
So, $E^\circ(\text{Au}^{3+}/\text{Au}^+) = +1.255$ V.

Now, calculate $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ for the disproportionation:
$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}$
$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ(\text{Au}^+/\text{Au}) - E^\circ(\text{Au}^{3+}/\text{Au}^+)$
$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.69 \text{ V} - 1.255 \text{ V} = +0.435$ V.

Answer: $+0.435$ V

A metal can displace another metal from its aqueous salt solution if it has a lower (more negative) standard reduction potential than the other metal.

- Metal R can displace only S (1 metal).
- Metal S has the highest $E^{\circ}$ and cannot displace any of the other metals (0 metals).

How much time is required to deposit 6.48 g of silver at the cathode when a current of 9.65 A is passed through an aqueous solution of silver nitrate?
(Given: Molar mass of $\mathrm{Ag} = 108 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}, 1 \mathrm{~F} = 96500 \mathrm{~C}$)
questions.question:
How much time is required to deposit 6.48 g of silver at the cathode when a current of 9.65 A is passed through an aqueous solution of silver nitrate?
(Given: Molar mass of $\mathrm{Ag} = 108 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}, 1 \mathrm{~F} = 96500 \mathrm{~C}$)
questions.solution:
The reduction reaction at the cathode for silver nitrate is:
$\mathrm{Ag}^{+} + \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{s})$

Here, the number of moles of electrons required per mole of Ag is $n = 1$.

According to Faraday's First Law of Electrolysis:
$w = \dfrac{M \times I \times t}{n \times F}$

Rearranging for time ($t$):
$t = \dfrac{w \times n \times F}{M \times I}$

Given:
$w = 6.48 \mathrm{~g}$
$M = 108 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
$I = 9.65 \mathrm{~A}$
$F = 96500 \mathrm{~C}$

Substituting the values into the equation:
$t = \dfrac{6.48 \times 1 \times 96500}{108 \times 9.65}$

$t = \dfrac{6.48}{108} \times 10000 = 0.06 \times 10000 = 600 \mathrm{~s}$

Converting the time into minutes:
Time in minutes = $\dfrac{600}{60} = 10 \mathrm{~min}$.

Answer: 10 min

questions.solution:
The given cell reaction is:
$\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{s})+2 \mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})+2 \mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{s})$

The number of moles of electrons transferred is $n = 2$.

The standard Gibbs energy change is:
$\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ} = -n \mathrm{F} \mathrm{E}_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}$
$-617.6 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} = -2 \times 96500 \mathrm{~C} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \times \mathrm{E}_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}$

$\mathrm{E}_{\text{cell}}^{\circ} = \dfrac{-617600}{-193000} \mathrm{~V} = 3.20 \mathrm{~V}$

The standard cell potential is also given by the difference in standard reduction potentials of the cathode and anode:
$\mathrm{E}_{\text{cell}}^{\circ} = \mathrm{E}_{\text{cathode}}^{\circ} - \mathrm{E}_{\text{anode}}^{\circ}$

Here, silver is reduced (cathode) and magnesium is oxidized (anode).
$3.20 \mathrm{~V} = \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+} / \mathrm{Ag}}^{\circ} - \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} / \mathrm{Mg}}^{\circ}$
$3.20 \mathrm{~V} = 0.80 \mathrm{~V} - \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} / \mathrm{Mg}}^{\circ}$

$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} / \mathrm{Mg}}^{\circ} = 0.80 \mathrm{~V} - 3.20 \mathrm{~V} = -2.40 \mathrm{~V}$

A sign error in the final step leads to $+2.40 \mathrm{~V}$. Assuming $n=1$ gives $-5.60 \mathrm{~V}$, and adding the potentials gives $+4.00 \mathrm{~V}$.

Answer: $-2.40 \mathrm{~V}$

questions.question: The limiting molar conductivities of $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$, $\text{BaCl}_2$ and $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ are given as $x$, $y$ and $z \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ respectively. The limiting molar conductivity of $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ in $\text{S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ will be:
questions.solution:
According to Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions:

$\Lambda_m^0(\text{Ba(OH)}_2) = \lambda^0_{\text{Ba}^{2+}} + 2\lambda^0_{\text{OH}^-} = x$
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{BaCl}_2) = \lambda^0_{\text{Ba}^{2+}} + 2\lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-} = y$
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}) = \lambda^0_{\text{NH}_4^+} + \lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-} = z$

Subtracting the second equation from the first gives:
$x - y = 2\lambda^0_{\text{OH}^-} - 2\lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-}$
$\Rightarrow \lambda^0_{\text{OH}^-} - \lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-} = \dfrac{x - y}{2}$

The limiting molar conductivity for $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ is:
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}) = \lambda^0_{\text{NH}_4^+} + \lambda^0_{\text{OH}^-}$

This can be rewritten as:
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}) = (\lambda^0_{\text{NH}_4^+} + \lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-}) + (\lambda^0_{\text{OH}^-} - \lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-})$
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}) = z + \dfrac{x - y}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{x - y}{2} + z$

$K_a = \dfrac{C\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}$

$K_a = \dfrac{0.018 \times 0.01}{0.9} = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{-4}}{0.9} = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}$

If the molar conductivity of a $0.001$ M solution of the weak acid $\text{HA}$ at the same temperature is $39.1$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$, what is its degree of dissociation?
questions.question: The plots of molar conductivity ($\Lambda_m$) versus the square root of concentration ($\sqrt{c}$) for the strong electrolytes $\text{HCl}$, $\text{NaA}$, and $\text{NaCl}$ yield straight lines with y-intercepts of $426.0$, $91.0$, and $126.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$, respectively, at $298$ K. If the molar conductivity of a $0.001$ M solution of the weak acid $\text{HA}$ at the same temperature is $39.1$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$, what is its degree of dissociation?
questions.solution:
For strong electrolytes, the y-intercept of the $\Lambda_m$ versus $\sqrt{c}$ plot corresponds to the limiting molar conductivity ($\Lambda_m^0$).

Thus, we have:
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{HCl}) = 426.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NaA}) = 91.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NaCl}) = 126.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$

According to Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions, the limiting molar conductivity of the weak acid $\text{HA}$ can be calculated as:

$\Lambda_m^0(\text{HA}) = \Lambda_m^0(\text{HCl}) + \Lambda_m^0(\text{NaA}) - \Lambda_m^0(\text{NaCl})$

$\Lambda_m^0(\text{HA}) = 426.0 + 91.0 - 126.0 = 391.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$

The degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) is given by the ratio of molar conductivity at a given concentration to the limiting molar conductivity:

$\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^0}$

$\alpha = \dfrac{39.1}{391.0} = 0.10$

Answer: $0.10$
